findings.title: GpuProfiler copies into the readback buffer every frame even while its map is pending, causing a BufferStillMapped panic on real GPUs
findings.claim: resolve() unconditionally records resolve_query_set plus copy_buffer_to_buffer into readback_buffer every frame. If the previous frame's map_async has not completed by the next poll_results, the buffer is still in the Waiting map state. queue.submit then fails with BufferStillMapped, and the default handler panics.
findings.derivation:
Per-frame order in render():
- poll_results at pipeline.rs:1404 does device.poll(Poll) and returns early if the callback has not fired, leaving readback_pending=true.
- resolve at 1592 has no readback_pending guard (gpu_timing.rs:157-173).
- submit at 1594.
- begin_readback at 1597 skips because readback_pending is still true.
wgpu-core 24.0.5 device/queue.rs:1519-1521: for every buffer used by the submitted command buffer, `match *buffer.map_state.lock() { BufferMapState::Idle => (), _ => return Err(QueueSubmitError::BufferStillMapped(..)) }`. Waiting is not Idle. wgpu-24.0.5 backend/wgpu_core.rs:1803-1807 routes the submit error to handle_error_nolabel, and default_error_handler (651-653) panics.
The trigger is that frame N's GPU work is unfinished at frame N+1's non-blocking poll. That is normal with desired_maximum_frame_latency=2 (pipeline.rs:355) whenever the GPU is the bottleneck, e.g. the branched-flow trace at high ray counts.
The profiler is active only when the adapter exposes TIMESTAMP_QUERY (pipeline.rs:308-317), which Vulkan/DX12/Metal adapters typically do. On GLES it requires GL_ARB_timer_query (wgpu-hal-24.0.4 gles/adapter.rs:475-479), so on the WSLg dev machine the profiler is most likely a no-op. That would explain why the bug has never been observed there. Not runtime-reproduced (no real GPU available).
findings.impact: An intermittent panic on real-GPU machines, most likely when GPU-bound (heavy branched flow, high resolution). It also cannot be caught in WSLg development.
findings.recommendation: In resolve(), return early when readback_pending is true (skip timing for that frame), or use a ring of 2-3 readback buffers indexed by frame. The wgpu-profiler crate implements exactly this pattern and could replace gpu_timing.rs. Also resolve only the query indices written this frame.

verification.reasoning:
The race is confirmed in code.
- resolve() (gpu_timing.rs:157-173) checks only self.enabled and always records copy_buffer_to_buffer into readback_buffer.
- poll_results returns early at 202-203 while readback_pending stays true. begin_readback skips at 178.
- Buffer::map_async sets map_state to Waiting (wgpu-core-24.0.5 resource.rs:506). validate_command_buffer (device/queue.rs:1516-1522) rejects any used buffer not Idle with BufferStillMapped.
- wgpu-24.0.5 wgpu_core.rs:1793-1807 routes submit errors to handle_error_nolabel, and default_error_handler (:650-653) panics.
- Frame order is pipeline.rs:1404 poll, then 1592 resolve, then 1594 submit, then 1597 begin_readback, as stated.
The derivation's premise about the dev machine is contradicted by evidence I can read:
- wgpu-hal-24.0.4 vulkan/adapter.rs:503-515 adds TIMESTAMP_QUERY to every Vulkan adapter, with no gate on timestampComputeAndGraphics.
- scratchpad/app_default.log:18-19 shows wgpu_hal::vulkan hiding both dzn adapters. Lines 20-29 show naga::back::spv::writer compiling the app's shaders, so a Vulkan adapter was selected. That is lavapipe, since lvp_icd.json is present, not GLES.
- pipeline.rs:308-317 therefore requests TIMESTAMP_QUERY, and the GpuProfiler is live on the WSLg dev machine today.
The statements 'most likely a no-op' and 'cannot be caught in WSLg development' are wrong. MEMORY.md's 'GLES software rendering' note is stale, which is likely why the finder assumed GLES. A probable reason the race is not seen is that the CPU rasterizer's software present finishes frame N before frame N+1's non-blocking poll [inference, not measured].
This finding is a strict subset of gpuperf-04, part 1.
verification.corrected_claim: The BufferStillMapped panic race is real and the code path is as described. However, the profiler is not a no-op on the dev machine: the app runs on Vulkan lavapipe (SPIR-V writer in app_default.log), and wgpu-hal 24 exposes TIMESTAMP_QUERY on every Vulkan adapter. The race is latent there, probably because CPU-rasterized frames complete before the next poll [inference]. It is expected to show intermittently on real GPUs when GPU time exceeds CPU frame time. This is a duplicate of gpuperf-04, part 1.

findings.title: Uncommitted 4x ray cut relies on 'temporal accumulation', but ray seeds are frame-invariant, so the 0.85 fade adds no sample density (#35 not done)
findings.claim: Ray start positions are hashed from ray_idx only, so every frame re-traces the same 8192 initial conditions. The 0.85 fade is an EMA over nearly identical images: steady-state gain 1/(1-0.85)=6.67x plus persistence, but no new rays. The uncommitted comment 'temporal accumulation (0.85 fade) builds up density over ~10 frames' is therefore false. The change permanently cuts distinct ray samples 4x (32768->8192) and ray-steps 8x (32768*400 -> 8192*200).
findings.derivation:
rg over branched_flow_compute.wgsl finds no use of params.time or any frame counter in the ray initialisation (lines 439-476). The only randomness is hash21(ray_idx-derived), and hash21 (222-226) is a pure function. So frame k traces the same rays as frame k-1. The only frame-to-frame changes are scatterer Brownian drift of about 0.001 UV per frame (branched_flow.rs:612) and slow thickness evolution.
EMA with lambda=0.85: S = sum lambda^k D = D/(1-lambda) = 6.67 D. That is a brightness gain, not added coverage.
If seeds varied per frame, the EMA variance factor would be (1-lambda)/(1+lambda) = 0.081, equivalent to (1+lambda)/(1-lambda) = 12.3 independent frames. 8192 rays/frame would then behave like about 100K rays, more than the old 32768 single-frame set, at zero extra cost.
Re the task note on #35: the fade pass exists (wgsl:559-569), but progressive temporal accumulation does not, so #35 is not effectively done.
findings.impact: With the uncommitted defaults, branch patterns are permanently 4x sparser in sample count. The cheaper frame is bought with lower image quality, not recovered by accumulation. The perf gain itself is real ([estimated] about 8x fewer ray-steps per frame).
findings.recommendation: Add a frame index to the hash seed, e.g. hash21(vec2(f32(ray_idx)*0.1, f32(frame_idx)*1.618)). Upload frame_idx in the unused params.time or a reserved field. Keep the 0.85 fade (or make lambda configurable). Fix the comment in branched_flow.rs:112, and update #35 to say the remaining work is per-frame seed variation.

findings.title: Recording mode drains the GPU each captured frame (poll Wait) and serializes on the previous frame's PNG encode
findings.claim: Every recorded frame blocks the render thread twice. It joins the previous frame's PNG thread before mapping, then calls device.poll(Maintain::Wait), a full CPU-GPU sync. It then un-pads and swizzles ~4-8 MB on the render thread, and export_frame copies the buffer again with to_vec. So recording throughput is min(render fps, 1/T_png) with no CPU-GPU overlap.
findings.derivation:
Code path: render() -> prepare_capture (copy to the single staging buffer) -> submit -> process_capture.
- join of the previous encoder thread (158-160).
- map_async + poll(Wait) (165-169).
- row copy + swap(0,2) on the render thread (176-188).
- spawn a new thread (201) that copies again (image_export.rs:66) and encodes with the default PNG compression.
With one staging buffer and one encoder thread, frame N+1 cannot start its readback until frame N's PNG finishes. PNG encode of a 1280x782 RGBA frame with image-0.25 default compression is [estimated, requires measurement] tens of ms, which would cap recording at roughly 15-50 fps. Not measured here.
findings.impact: Only while recording (F11/UI) or taking a screenshot; the normal render loop is unaffected. On WSLg the poll(Wait) also waits on llvmpipe.
findings.recommendation: Use a ring of 2-3 staging buffers: map_async, then check with poll(Poll) on later frames. Send ownership of the pixel Vec over a bounded channel to a persistent encoder thread or pool, and drop to_vec by passing the Vec into ImageBuffer::from_raw. Use PngEncoder with CompressionType::Fast for recording, and do the un-pad/swizzle on the worker thread.

findings.title: GPU drainage computes step_dt but never uploads it; time_scale is dead and the displayed sim time is ~167x off
findings.claim: step() derives step_dt = frame_dt*time_scale/steps_per_frame but uses it only to advance current_time. The shader integrates with params.dt, fixed at 0.001 s, and set_dt has no callers. So the GPU drainage time_scale slider (ui_state.rs:352) changes only the clock display, and physics advances per frame rather than per second.
findings.derivation:
rg finds set_dt/update_params/set_physics/set_bubble_radius on GPUDrainageSimulator never called outside gpu_drainage.rs. params.dt stays at its default 0.001 (gpu_drainage.rs:49).
Per frame: physics advances steps*0.001 = 0.01 s (default steps=10), while the clock advances frame_dt*100 = 1.667 s at 60 fps. Ratio 167x at 60 fps, 1000x at 10 fps (WSLg).
The physics wall-clock rate is 0.01 s/frame, so it is 6x slower at 10 fps than at 60 fps.
docs/key-insights.md:779-784 says 'GPU drainage runs faster than real-time ... time_scale 100x', which is doc drift. Memory item #31 ('actual frame dt for drainage dispatch') is only half done.
CFL trap for the fix: the GPU grid matches the CPU one (128 theta x 256 phi, R=0.025, D=1e-9). Explicit phi-diffusion at row 1 needs dt <= R^2 sin^2(dtheta) dphi^2/(2D) = 0.115 s (computed). Naively uploading step_dt = 0.167 s (60 fps, scale 100, 10 steps) would destabilize row 1, as cpuperf-06 shows for the CPU solver.
Also, GPU bubble_radius is hard-coded at 0.025 (gpu_drainage.rs:54) and set_bubble_radius is never called, so --diameter does not reach GPU drainage.
findings.impact: The time-scale UI does nothing physically, the reported drainage time is wrong by two to three orders of magnitude, and simulated drainage speed depends on frame rate (WSLg vs real GPU).
findings.recommendation: Each frame, compute scaled_dt and set steps = ceil(scaled_dt / dt_max) with dt_max of about 0.1 s (or a polar-row CFL estimate), capped at a max-steps budget, then write params.dt = scaled_dt/steps before dispatch. Advance current_time by steps*params.dt. Sync bubble_radius from SimulationConfig. Fix docs/key-insights.md:779-784.

verification.reasoning: Same root cause as drainage-02 (dedupe). Verified: step_dt (gpu_drainage.rs:355) is used only for current_time (:376), set_dt has no callers, params.dt = 0.001 (:49), bubble_radius is hard-coded at 0.025 (:54), and set_bubble_radius is never called, so --diameter does not reach GPU drainage. The 167x and 1000x clock-vs-nominal ratios check (1.667 s against 10×0.001 s). One caveat: 'physics advances 0.01 s per frame' is only nominal. Per drainage-02 the f32 update is sub-half-ulp, so the field does not change at all. The row-1 CFL limit of 0.115 s checks, and key-insights.md:780 says 'GPU drainage runs faster than real-time'. Severity raised to match drainage-02.

findings.title: CPU drainage: one explicit-Euler step per frame with dt = frame_dt*100 exceeds the polar stability limit about 14x and blows up
findings.claim: RenderPipeline::update advances DrainageSimulator by a single forward-Euler step of dt = frame_dt*drainage_time_scale (default 100), i.e. 1.667 s at 60 fps. The phi-diffusion term D/(R^2 sin^2 theta) makes the near-pole rows unstable for dt > 0.115 s (row 1), so any phi-asymmetric perturbation grows by up to |1-4D dt/(R^2 sin^2 theta dphi^2)| = 28x per frame. TFE fronts, on by default, supply the asymmetry.
findings.derivation:
Analytic: FTCS on the phi direction is stable iff D dt * 2/(R^2 sin^2 theta_k dphi^2) <= 1. With R=0.025, D=1e-9 (config default), nt=128 (dtheta=pi/127), nphi=256: dt_max = 0.115 s at row 1, 0.46 s at row 2, 1.04 s at row 3, 1.84 s at row 4. At 60 fps dt=1.667 s violates rows 1-3; at 10 fps (WSLg) dt=10 s violates rows 1-9. Stability requires fps > 870.
Rust replica (bench_stab.rs, same f64 loop as drainage.rs:291-386, TFE off): a 1e-12 relative seed at row 1 grows to a deviation of 2.1e2 m by step 24 and 6.1e10 m by step 60 at 60 fps. At 144 fps it reaches 5e4 m by step 48. At dt=0.1 s (below the bound) it decays (2e-20 m at step 60). A seed in stable row 5 leaks to row 1 and blows up by step 48.
Full numpy port with TFE on (drainage.rs:277 default): blow-up (>10 um) first at frame 25 (60 fps) and frame 12 (10 fps), with peaks of 2.7e-3 m and 5.6e5 m. Cells then clamp to 0 and freeze below critical (drainage.rs:326): after 80 frames, 24% (60 fps) and 79% (10 fps) of cells are below 10 nm.
With TFE off and an exactly uniform field it stays stable, because bit-identical rows have nothing to amplify.
Measured cost (standalone replica, rustc -O, min-of-N, load avg 16 on 8 cores): 0.42-0.46 ms/step at 128x256, plus 55 us for the three full scans per frame (min_thickness, max_thickness, and has_critical_region rescanning, pipeline.rs:1301-1318).
findings.impact: Only when 'physics drainage' is enabled (off by default). The corrupted min/max feed bubble_uniform.drainage_speed = 1 - min/max (pipeline.rs:1314-1315), which saturates. has_critical_region then fires log::info! every frame (pipeline.rs:1318-1323) under the default 'info' filter (main.rs:206), about 60 log lines/s. On WSLg's low fps the blow-up appears in half the frames. Parallelizing (rayon) is moot until the scheme is stable.
findings.recommendation: Replace frame-coupled stepping with a fixed-dt accumulator and CFL-limited substeps (needs about 15 substeps/frame at 60 fps x100, i.e. [estimated] 6 ms single-threaded; then rayon par_chunks over theta rows becomes worthwhile). Better: treat the phi direction implicitly (cyclic tridiagonal per row, O(nphi)) or apply a polar Fourier filter, the standard lat-lon fix. Alternatively drop the CPU path from the interactive loop in favour of the GPU solver. Compute min/max inside the step loop and rate-limit the 'would burst' log. Hand the TFE unbounded-thinning issue to the physics dimension (see open_questions).

verification.reasoning: Duplicate of drainage-01 (dedupe). The FTCS φ-limit dt ≤ R^2 sin^2θ dφ^2/(2D) = 0.115 s at row 1 checks, and rows 2-4 come out at 0.46, 1.04 and 1.84 s. At 10 fps, dt = 10 s violates rows 1-9 (row k ≈ 0.115k^2), which checks. fps > 870 also checks. has_critical_region logs at info every frame (pipeline.rs:1318-1323, default 'info' filter at main.rs:206). The '0.42-0.46 ms/step' figure is a measurement of a standalone replica on a loaded machine, not of the project binary, and is unverified here. The blow-up frame numbers are replica outputs. Raised to high because a solver that diverges within seconds when enabled is high, not medium, even for an opt-in feature.

findings.title: current_thickness_buffer()/concentration_buffer() return the input of the last sub-step (off-by-one); the claimed stale-read fix is still one step stale
findings.claim: After step(), the most recent output is thickness_buffers[current_buffer], which is also the next input. The accessor returns [1 - current_buffer], the buffer that was the read-only input of the final dispatch, so consumers always see state one sub-step (1 ms simulated) old. concentration_buffer() (line 490) has the same bug.
findings.code_quote:
gpu_drainage.rs:504  &self.thickness_buffers[1 - self.current_buffer]
gpu_drainage.rs:490  &self.concentration_buffers[1 - self.current_buffer]
findings.derivation:
bind_groups[0] reads buf0 and writes buf1; bind_groups[1] reads buf1 and writes buf0 (gpu_drainage.rs:245-300). After dispatching with index c, current_buffer becomes 1-c and the written buffer is buf[1-c] = buf[current_buffer]. The comment at 502-503 inverts this.
Simulated in pingpong.py for steps_per_frame in {10, 9, 1}: the accessor always lags the latest output by exactly 1 step. With an even steps_per_frame (default 10) it returns buf1 every frame.
In a 2-buffer ping-pong, either buffer is at most one step stale, so the never-rebuilt caustic bind group (caustics.rs:212-222, bound to buf1 at init) is exactly as fresh as the rebuilt branched-flow one. CLAUDE.md:82-84 ('rebuilt each frame ... to prevent stale reads') overstates what the rebuild achieves.
findings.impact: Visually negligible (1 ms of simulated time). It matters because the per-frame rebuild built on this premise is redundant (cpuperf-08), and the doc claim is inaccurate.
findings.recommendation: Return &self.thickness_buffers[self.current_buffer] (and likewise for concentration), fix the comment, and update CLAUDE.md's 'Stale buffer prevention' paragraph.

findings.title: Per-frame branched-flow create_bind_group can be replaced by two cached bind groups; drainage's 10 passes can be one
findings.claim: Only binding 1 (thickness) ever changes, and it alternates between exactly two buffers. Caching [BindGroup; 2], indexed by GPUDrainageSimulator::current_buffer after the cpuperf-07 fix, gives identical correctness with zero per-frame creation. Separately, GPUDrainageSimulator::step opens steps_per_frame (10) separate compute passes where one pass with 10 dispatches would do.
findings.derivation:
Bindings 0, 2, 3 and 4 (params, caustic, scatterer and cell_offsets buffers) are created once and never replaced. Binding 1 is thickness_buffers[0|1]. With the default even steps_per_frame, the rebuilt bind group is the same every frame (pingpong.py), so the rebuild is pure overhead.
wgpu tracks usage scopes per dispatch inside a compute pass and inserts the needed barriers between dispatches, so merging the 10 drainage passes keeps correctness.
Cost of create_bind_group plus deferred destruction: [estimated, requires measurement] about 5-30 us/frame on Vulkan/DX12 (descriptor alloc + update), about 1-2 us on GLES (CPU-side binding list). Per-pass begin/end overhead: [estimated] a few us each.
findings.impact: Small: [estimated] well under 1% of a 16.7 ms frame on a real GPU; irrelevant on WSLg/GLES. It is mostly cleanup that removes per-frame object churn.
findings.recommendation: Build both bind groups in BranchedFlowSimulator::new from gpu_drainage's two thickness buffers (expose thickness_buffers or a by-index accessor), select by index in step(), and delete rebuild_bind_group. Do the same for CausticRenderer::compute_bind_group. In GPUDrainageSimulator::step, open one compute pass and loop set_bind_group/dispatch_workgroups inside it.

findings.title: Cargo profiles: dependencies unoptimized in dev; fat LTO costs about 2 min per release build for a CPU path under 1 ms per frame
findings.claim: Only [profile.release] (opt-level=3, lto=true i.e. fat) is set. There is no [profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level, so `cargo run` (CLAUDE.md's default run command) and `cargo test` run wgpu-core, naga, egui and image unoptimized with debug assertions. There is also no codegen-units=1, and there is no .cargo/config.toml. The CPU-side hot code is tiny (measured 17 us scatterers, about 0.45 ms CPU drainage only when enabled), so fat LTO buys little runtime.
findings.code_quote:
Cargo.toml:41-43  [profile.release]
opt-level = 3
lto = true
findings.derivation: Measured per-frame CPU work in the replica bench is far below frame time, so the binary is GPU/driver/egui bound and whole-program LTO has little to optimize [estimated]. Project memory records LTO release builds of about 2 minutes (not re-measured; cargo was locked). Debug builds of wgpu-core/naga are notoriously slow at shader compile and validation, which affects every `cargo run` without --release and the naga WSGL validation tests [estimated]. target-cpu=native is not recommended: it hurts portability for negligible gain on this workload.
findings.impact: Developer iteration time and debug-run frame rate. Release runtime is essentially unaffected.
findings.recommendation: Add `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 3` (optionally `[profile.dev] opt-level = 1`). Consider `lto = "thin"` plus `codegen-units = 1`, or a separate `[profile.dist]` with fat LTO for distribution builds. Measure both on a real GPU before choosing.

findings.title: Drainage sims ignore the user's SimulationConfig (CPU path built from Default; GPU radius hard-coded); #29 only partly done
findings.claim: Enabling physics drainage from the UI builds DrainageSimulator from SimulationConfig::default(), not the --config/--diameter/--thickness config that RenderPipeline::new received. GPU drainage keeps bubble_radius=0.025 because set_bubble_radius is never called. The resolved-#29 note ('Propagate SimulationConfig to both pipelines') is therefore incomplete for the drainage solvers.
findings.code_quote:
pipeline.rs:1749  let config = SimulationConfig::default();
gpu_drainage.rs:54  bubble_radius: 0.025,      // 2.5cm radius
findings.derivation: RenderPipeline::new takes sim_config (pipeline.rs:279) but does not store it in the struct (fields 186-267), so apply_ui_changes must fall back to Default at 1749. rg finds no caller of GPUDrainageSimulator::set_bubble_radius. Laplacian coefficients scale as 1/R^2 (drainage.rs:351, drainage.wgsl:68), so a --diameter 0.08 run uses the wrong surface Laplacian in both solvers.
findings.impact: Drainage results and stability limits do not follow CLI/config bubble size, thickness or fluid parameters.
findings.recommendation: Store the SimulationConfig (or the needed fields) in RenderPipeline. Use it in init_drainage_simulator, and call gpu_drainage.set_bubble_radius(config.bubble_radius()) plus set_physics(...) at init.

findings.title: GpuProfiler doc claims drainage/caustic/render timings, but only branched-flow passes are instrumented
findings.claim: Module docs and GpuTimingResults expose drainage_ms, caustic_ms and render_ms, but only BranchedFlowClear/Trace pass timestamp writes. The other three fields are always 0, so the overlay's GPU timing undercounts.
findings.derivation: compute_pass_timestamps is called only at pipeline.rs:1430-1435 (BranchedFlowClear/Trace). The drainage passes (gpu_drainage.rs:365), the caustic pass (caustics.rs:448) and the main render pass (pipeline.rs:1487) pass timestamp_writes: None. render_pass_timestamps (gpu_timing.rs:142) has no callers.
findings.impact: Misleading profiling numbers on real GPUs; the bottleneck attribution in the overlay is incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Wire the Drainage (first/last pass), Caustic and Render timestamps, or remove those fields and fix the doc comment. Consider adopting the wgpu-profiler crate (see cpuperf-02).

findings.title: Deformation slider does not update the patch mesh (patch view keeps the old aspect ratio)
findings.claim: set_deformation regenerates only the full-sphere mesh. The patch mesh (the default view when branched flow is on) is rebuilt with self.aspect_ratio only when the patch center or size changes, so toggling deformation has no effect in patch view.
findings.derivation: regenerate_patch_mesh is called only from apply_ui_changes when patch_params_changed (pipeline.rs:1840-1848). set_deformation (908-925) does not call it.
findings.impact: Visual inconsistency only; no performance effect.
findings.recommendation: Call self.regenerate_patch_mesh() at the end of set_deformation.

findings.title: Scatterer loop dominates the trace kernel: ~170 scatterers examined per ray-step in patch mode (doc claims 10-30); precompute a per-frame force field
findings.claim: Default patch mode puts all 400 scatterers into the 0.316x0.316 UV patch (branched_flow.rs:590-606), which the fixed 10x10 grid covers with only ~4x4 cells. The 3x3-cell lookup therefore visits about 170 scatterers per ray-step, of which about 70 are inside the 3-sigma cutoff. This is not the O(k), k about 10-30, claimed at wgsl:88 and CLAUDE.md:88. In full-sphere mode it visits 35 (10.4 inside the cutoff). The summed force is a smooth field over UV that does not depend on the ray, so recomputing it per ray per step repeats the same work about 25x.
findings.derivation: Counted in a numpy replica of wgsl:405-553 with branched_flow.rs defaults (8192 rays, 200 steps, 400 scatterers, patch 0.5/0.5/0.158, sigma 0.03, pw 0.1) and GRIN=0, since the field is exactly uniform (gpuperf-03). Patch mode: mean 169.7 scatterers examined per step, 69.6 inside the cutoff. Full mode: 35.1 and 10.4. Evaluations per frame = 8192*200*169.7 = 278M. Geometric check: the rays sit at local u about 0.9, so the neighbourhood covers cells 5-7 by 4-6, about 0.158x0.258 UV of the patch, giving 0.0408*400/0.0999 = 163, which matches. Alternative: one compute pass that writes F(u,v) = (1-pw)*grad_h + pw*sum F_s into a 256x256 patch-local (or 512x256 UV) vec2 grid costs 65,536 texels * about 170-266 = 11-17M evaluations, about 16-25x fewer. Each ray step then needs 4 vec2 loads (or 1 filtered fetch with FLOAT32_FILTERABLE/rg16float) instead of 16 thickness loads + 2 offset loads + about 170 scatterer loads. Interpolation error: texel h = 0.316/256 = 0.0012 UV against sigma = 0.03, so h/sigma = 0.04 and the bilinear error is about (h/sigma)^2/8, roughly 2e-4 relative. Per-step instruction count drops by about 10x [estimated, requires measurement]. The SIMD cost of the variable inner trip count is negligible: the replica gives warp efficiency mean(k)/mean(warp-max k) = 0.998. Side issues: the cutoff radius 3*sigma_max = 3*0.036 = 0.108 exceeds GRID_CELL_SIZE 0.1, so the 3x3 lookup can miss a scatterer whose force is up to about 10% of peak. The grid also does not wrap u (phi is periodic) in full-sphere mode.
findings.impact: Largest per-step cost in the dominant GPU pass on both llvmpipe and real GPUs. The documented complexity is wrong by about 10x in the default (patch) mode.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'force_field' compute pass that runs after update_scatterers and before trace, with the GRIN gradient (including the spherical metric and thickness_scale) and the particle forces folded into one vec2 grid. Make the trace step a single interpolated fetch. This changes the propagation loop body, which CLAUDE.md:111-113 forbids (see gpuperf-08). Validate first on the Dozen/Vulkan adapter or natively, with a small ray count, and compare deposit images against the current kernel. Fix the doc complexity claim. If the grid stays, set GRID_CELL_SIZE >= 3*sigma_max and make the cells patch-local.

- Defaults are 8192 rays, 200 steps, 400 scatterers, sigma 0.03, pw 0.1, patch 0.5/0.5/0.158 (branched_flow.rs:113-142).

- pos_3d = normalize(1,0,1), so phi = pi/4 and u = 0.625, i.e. patch-local u of about 0.90. This matches 'local u about 0.9'.

(b) The field is not exactly smooth. The hard 3-sigma cutoff (wgsl:309) and the 3x3-cell truncation are discontinuous, so a precomputed grid changes output and is not a pure refactor.
(c) 'Largest cost in the dominant GPU pass' is unmeasured. Also, branched flow is off by default (branched_flow.rs:496 enabled:false) and needs gpu_drainage_enabled (default false, pipeline.rs:813). 'Default mode' means default parameters once the user enables it.

Full mode examines about 35 (about 10 inside). The force field is ray-independent per frame, and a precomputed grid would cut evaluations about 16-25x [estimated]. findings.title: u32 fixed-point deposit truncation discards ~57% of deposited energy; the 256->64 scale reduction was unnecessary
findings.claim: Each deposit is about 64*0.15*0.3*I, roughly 2.9 units, split bilinearly over 4 texels and truncated with u32(). Most corners become 0. Overflow is nowhere near: steady-state maxima are about 1e4, against a u32 limit of 4.29e9.
findings.derivation: step_factor is pinned at 0.3 (gpuperf-05), so D = 64*0.15*0.3*~0.9 = 2.6. Each corner gets floor(D*w) with w averaging 0.25, which is mostly 0 or 1. Numpy replica, patch mode, scale 64: 42.9% of the ideal sum is deposited and 75.1% of corner deposits truncate to 0. Full mode: 43.3% and 74.9%. Same replica at scale 4096: 98.8% deposited and 3.7% zeroed. Overflow bound: the clear pass gives S_{n+1} = 0.85*S_n + D_n, so the steady state is D/0.15 = 6.67*D. Largest single-frame texel value in the replica: 2001 at scale 64, so steady state is 1.33e4. At scale 4096 it is 288,844, steady state 1.93e6, about 2200x below 4.29e9. Even 8x more rays/steps or a 100x hotter caustic stays below the limit. Commit 5da4fbc's 'Reduce atomicAdd deposit scale 256->64 to prevent overflow' therefore fixed a problem that did not exist and made the truncation 4x worse. The clear pass floors as well: u32(f32(v)*0.85) takes v<=6 down by exactly 1 per frame, an extra fade on faint texels.
findings.impact: Branch brightness is about 2.3x too low. Weak bilinear corners vanish, which aliases the splat into a thresholded near-nearest-neighbour stamp and shows as grain or broken filaments. The loss is worst exactly where strong forces shrink steps.
findings.recommendation: Raise the scale to 4096, or 1024 if ray counts may exceed about 64K, and change the decode '/ 64.0' in bubble.wgsl:272-275 in lockstep. Expect visible intensity to rise about 2.3x, so re-tune branched_flow_intensity. Alternatively keep 64 and use round-to-nearest or hash-dithered stochastic rounding. Add a test that ties the encode and decode constants together.

verification.reasoning: Duplicate of branched-07. Truncation at :395-398 verified. With D ≈ 2.6 (intensity about 0.9), the analytic kept fraction is 4·[P(w≥0.385) + P(w≥0.769)]/2.6 = 4·(0.248 + 0.029)/2.6 = 0.426, consistent with the stated 42.9%. Fade floor: u32(0.85v) drops small values faster than 0.85 (v=1→0, v=2→1, v=3→2, v=4→3, v=5→4, v=6→5). The overflow-headroom figures are replica-based and unverified here. A pathological all-rays-on-one-texel bound could approach u32 limits, so 'did not exist' holds for realistic loads only. The 5da4fbc commit message was not verified. Medium to match branched-07, because the loss is a global brightness factor plus aliasing and can be partly compensated by the intensity slider.

findings.title: GRIN path computes exactly zero: drainage dt never reaches the GPU, the f32 update is below 1 ulp, and thickness_scale is never applied
findings.claim: GPUDrainageSimulator::step() computes step_dt but never uploads it, and set_dt() has no callers, so the shader always uses dt=0.001 s. The #31 fix (commit e253dfb) passes last_dt into step(), but the value goes nowhere. At dt=1e-3 the per-step change in h is 3-5 orders of magnitude below the f32 ulp of 500 nm, so the field stays exactly uniform and its Laplacian is exactly 0. thickness_gradient_uv therefore returns 0, and the 16 storage loads per ray-step, the 10 drainage passes per frame and the caustic pass all compute nothing. The branched-flow shader also never multiplies by thickness_scale (1e6; declared at wgsl:38, never read), so even a non-uniform field in metres bends rays by about 1e-6 rad.
findings.derivation: drainage.wgsl:142-147,170: dh/dt = -(rho g/3 eta) h^3 sin(theta) = -3.27e6 * (5e-7)^3 * sin(theta), at most -4.09e-13 m/s. At dt=1e-3 the increment is -4.1e-16 m. ulp(f32 5e-7) = 2^-44 = 5.68e-14 m. Numpy float32 confirms h + dt*dhdt == h at theta = 10, 45 and 90 deg (f32_drainage.py). Even with dt plumbed, (1/60)*100/10 = 0.167 s gives -6.8e-14 m, about 1.2 ulp, so the update is badly quantized. A uniform initial field (pipeline.rs:708-712, vec![initial; n] at gpu_drainage.rs:127) has an f32 Laplacian of exactly 0.0, so it never becomes non-uniform. GRIN scale: for a hypothetical dh/dv = 200 nm per UV unit, the force is 1.8e-7, the turn per step is 5*1.8e-7*0.015 = 1.35e-8 rad, and over 200 steps 2.7e-6 rad. With the 1e6 scale applied it is 2.7 rad. Plumbing details: current_buffer() returns buffers[1-current], which is always the input of the last sub-step and one sub-step stale (bufidx.py, every steps_per_frame). The caustic compute bind group is built once at caustics.rs:212-222 and is never rebuilt, so it stays bound to buffer 1: current for odd steps_per_frame, one sub-step stale for even. caustics_compute.wgsl likewise never applies film_thickness_scale. The drainage_term has units of m^2/s, not m/s (it is missing a spatial derivative). That point belongs to the math auditor and is noted here only for completeness.
findings.impact: The visible branched flow is driven purely by particle scatterers. The GRIN model in CLAUDE.md and the docs is inactive. GPU time goes to 10 drainage passes, a caustic pass and 16 loads per ray-step that change nothing. The #31 resolution recorded in MEMORY.md does not hold.
findings.recommendation: Upload dt each frame through set_dt or a write_buffer in step(), and check stability first: the pole rows have a 1/(sin^2(theta) dphi^2) factor, so a naive 0.17 s step may be explicitly unstable. Store the deviation dh = h - h0 rather than h, or seed a non-uniform field, so f32 can resolve increments. Apply thickness_scale before the gradient, and film_thickness_scale in caustics. Until then, skip thickness_gradient_uv when the field is uniform, or fold it into gpuperf-01's force field. Fix current_buffer() to return buffers[current_buffer], and rebuild the caustic bind group per frame as is done for branched flow.

verification.reasoning: Core claims verified (dedupe with drainage-02 and branched-01): dt is never uploaded, the f32 update is below ulp, and thickness_scale is never applied. Stale-buffer claim checked independently: bind_groups[cb] reads buffers[cb] and writes buffers[1-cb] (gpu_drainage.rs:247-299), then current_buffer toggles (:375). After the step the newest data is buffers[current_buffer], but current_buffer() returns buffers[1-current_buffer] (:504), which is the input of the last sub-step. The comment at :502-503 is wrong. The caustic bind group is built once (caustics.rs:212) on the initial current_thickness_buffer(), which is buffer 1. 16 storage loads per ray-step (4 samples × 4 loads) checks. Minor numeric corrections: the per-step change is 0.0072 ulp at the equator, about 2 orders of magnitude below 1 ulp, rising to about 3 near the poles, not '3-5 orders'. With odd steps_per_frame the caustic buffer alternates between current and one sub-step stale on successive frames, rather than being 'current'. Neither changes the conclusion. All of this is latent while the field is invariant.

findings.title: GpuProfiler will panic or misuse Vulkan on any real GPU: copies into a map-pending buffer and resolves never-written queries
findings.claim: resolve() records copy_buffer_to_buffer into readback_buffer every frame. poll_results() returns early when the previous map_async has not completed, leaving that buffer in a map-pending state. wgpu-core 24.0.5 then rejects the submit with BufferStillMapped, and the default uncaptured-error handler panics (the project sets no on_uncaptured_error). Separately, resolve_query_set covers all 16 query slots, but only the BranchedFlowClear and BranchedFlowTrace slots (4 of 16) are ever written. wgpu 24 resets only the indices it writes and copies with VK_QUERY_RESULT_WAIT, so Vulkan copies uninitialized queries, which is invalid usage. Both bugs are hidden today only because WSL GLES/llvmpipe does not enable the profiler.
findings.code_quote:
encoder.resolve_query_set(query_set, 0..MAX_TIMESTAMPS, resolve_buf, 0);
        encoder.copy_buffer_to_buffer(
            resolve_buf,
            0,
            readback_buf,
findings.derivation: Frame order in pipeline.rs: get_current_texture (1360), then poll_results (1404), then resolve (1592), then submit (1594), then begin_readback (1597). poll_results at gpu_timing.rs:202-203 returns early if !map_ready, leaving readback_pending=true. resolve() at 157-173 checks only self.enabled. wgpu-core-24.0.5/src/device/queue.rs:1519-1521 rejects any used buffer whose map_state is not Idle with QueueSubmitError::BufferStillMapped. wgpu-24.0.5/src/backend/wgpu_core.rs:1803-1807 routes the error to handle_error_nolabel, and :651-653 default_error_handler panics. With desired_maximum_frame_latency 2 (pipeline.rs:355) the CPU can start frame N+1 before the GPU finishes frame N, so the race is live whenever frames are GPU-bound. Queries: wgpu-hal-24.0.4 vulkan/command.rs:410-418 uses QueryResultFlags::TYPE_64 | WAIT. vulkan/device.rs:2191-2221 creates the pool without resetting it. wgpu-core query.rs resets indices only on write (lines 208, 241, 292), and resolve has 'TODO(#3993): Need to track initialization state'. Only GpuPass::BranchedFlowClear/Trace are requested (pipeline.rs:1430-1435). drainage (gpu_drainage.rs:365), caustic and render pass timestamp_writes: None, so CLAUDE.md:93 and 5da4fbc's '5 named passes' overstate the coverage.
findings.impact: As soon as #38 is solved (Dozen/Vulkan, native Windows or Linux), TIMESTAMP_QUERY is reported and the profiler turns itself on. The app can then panic intermittently on GPU-bound frames, and on Vulkan it issues invalid query copies that may return garbage or lose the device.
findings.recommendation: Treat this as a prerequisite for any real-GPU benchmarking. Skip resolve and copy while readback_pending is set (or rotate 2-3 readback buffers). Resolve only the query ranges written this frame (keep a bitmask), or write timestamps for every GpuPass. Consider an on_uncaptured_error handler that logs instead of panicking for profiling paths.

verification.reasoning:
Part 1 (BufferStillMapped) is confirmed exactly as in cpuperf-02: gpu_timing.rs:157-173, 193-204; wgpu-core-24.0.5 resource.rs:506 sets Waiting; queue.rs:1516-1522 rejects non-Idle; wgpu-24.0.5 wgpu_core.rs:1793-1807 and :650-653 panic. cpuperf-02 is a strict subset of this finding.
Part 2 (queries) is confirmed in code:
- resolve_query_set(0..MAX_TIMESTAMPS=16) at gpu_timing.rs:12 and 165.
- The only timestamp writers are branched_flow.rs:728/741, requested at pipeline.rs:1430-1435 inside the branch at 1417, gated on branched_flow_simulator.enabled && gpu_drainage_enabled. Both default to false (branched_flow.rs:496, pipeline.rs:813). Drainage, caustic, render and egui passes all use timestamp_writes: None (gpu_drainage.rs:365, caustics.rs:448, pipeline.rs:1487, 1566).
- wgpu-hal-24.0.4 vulkan/device.rs:2191-2224 creates the pool with no reset. wgpu-core-24.0.5 device/resource.rs:3651-3696 adds no reset. query.rs:208/241/292 reset only on write. query.rs:440 carries the TODO(#3993) note.
- vulkan/command.rs:410-418 copies with TYPE_64|WAIT.
Two corrections:
(a) In the default configuration zero of 16 queries are ever written, not 4, yet all 16 are resolved and copied every frame. With branched flow on, 4 of 16 (indices 4-7) are written.
(b) 'Hidden today only because WSL GLES/llvmpipe does not enable the profiler' is wrong. wgpu-hal 24 vulkan/adapter.rs:509 exposes TIMESTAMP_QUERY on every Vulkan adapter. app_default.log:20-29 (naga spv writer) shows the app already runs on a Vulkan adapter (lavapipe; dzn is hidden at :18-19). So the profiler is live today and these uninitialized-query copies already execute every frame on lavapipe without visible failure in that (short) log. Whether a real NVIDIA driver hangs or returns garbage on WAIT over never-reset queries is unverified; it is invalid usage per the Vulkan spec.
The doc-coverage point is partly misattributed. CLAUDE.md:93 says only 'GPU timestamp profiling via GpuProfiler'. The overstatement is gpu_timing.rs:3-4 ('drainage, caustic, branched flow, and render passes') and the 5-variant GpuPass enum. The 5da4fbc commit-message quote is unverifiable without git.
verification.corrected_claim: Both bugs are confirmed in code. The readback-buffer race can panic with BufferStillMapped. resolve_query_set copies all 16 slots every frame while at most 4 are ever written, and in the default configuration (branched flow and GPU drainage off) none are. The bugs are not hidden by GLES: the app already runs on Vulkan lavapipe with the profiler enabled, and no failure has been observed there [lavapipe tolerance and timing are inferred]. On real Vulkan GPUs the uninitialized-query WAIT copy is spec-invalid, with unverified consequences. The over-documentation of coverage is in gpu_timing.rs:3-4, not CLAUDE.md:93.

findings.title: Adaptive step is pinned at the 0.3x clamp for ~97-100% of steps; rays travel only 0.3 tangent units, and the uncommitted comment claims the opposite
findings.claim: The threshold |F|*10 >= 3.33 is crossed by almost every step because a single scatterer at 1 sigma already gives |F| about 1.0 after particle_weight. The step is therefore always 0.3*0.005 = 0.0015, about 2.6 steps per output texel, and the 'adaptive' scheme is a constant 0.3x slowdown. The uncommitted comment at branched_flow.rs:114, 'adaptive stepping (0.3-3x) extends effective range', is wrong: the effective range is 200*0.0015 = 0.3 units, about 17 degrees. Both break conditions are dead with the defaults, so every ray runs all ray_steps.
findings.code_quote: let step_factor = clamp(1.0 / max(gradient_mag * 10.0, 0.333), 0.3, 3.0);
findings.derivation: Single scatterer at r = sigma: |F| = 0.5*2*(1/(2*0.03^2))*0.03*e^-0.5 = 10.1, times pw 0.1 gives 1.01 > 0.333. At r = 2 sigma it is still 0.45. Replica: fraction of steps at the 0.3 clamp is 0.996 (patch) and 0.968 (full). |F| percentiles p5/p50/p95 = 0.96/4.23/9.88. Median turn per step = 5*4.23*0.3*0.005 = 0.032 rad. Patch-local texel = 0.316*2pi/512, about 0.0039 rad in u (0.316*pi/256, about 0.0039 in v), so 0.0015 per step is about 2.6 deposits per texel crossed. Dead breaks: intensity 0.999^200 = 0.82 > 0.01, and max travel 0.3 is far below dist 2.5. A step of about 1 texel (0.004) gives a turn of 5*4.23*0.004 = 0.085 rad per step, which is adequate for smooth Gaussians (sigma is about 24-47 steps), so the same path needs about 2.6x fewer steps [estimated].
findings.impact: About 2.6x more steps than needed for a given path length on any backend. Ray range is also limited, which hides branching development: the 400->200 ray_steps change halved an already short path.
findings.recommendation: Replace the heuristic with a turning-angle limit, dt = clamp(theta_max/(bend_strength*|F|), dt_min, dt_texel), with theta_max about 0.05-0.1 rad and dt_texel about 1 output texel. Keep the step_factor deposit weighting, which correctly makes energy proportional to path length. Fix the comment in the uncommitted diff (branched_flow.rs:112-115) and in CLAUDE.md:89.

findings.title: #37 is the wrong lever: 8192 rays fill ~12% of an RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU; larger workgroups would idle SMs; the 32K->8K cut was tuned for llvmpipe
findings.claim: The dispatch is 8192/64 = 128 workgroups. The target GPU on this machine (vulkaninfo: RTX 3070 Ti Laptop, GA104, 46 SMs, at most 48 warps per SM) gets about 5.6 warps per SM, roughly 12% occupancy, and the dependent per-step memory chain makes the kernel latency-bound. Workgroup size 128 gives 64 WGs (max 2 per SM against a mean of 1.39, about 70% balance), and 256 gives 32 WGs, fewer than 46 SMs, leaving 14 idle. The uncommitted 4x ray cut therefore probably saves far less than 4x on real hardware while quartering sample density. On llvmpipe, which is throughput-bound, it does save about 4x.
findings.code_quote:
let workgroups = self.params.num_rays.div_ceil(64);
            pass.dispatch_workgroups(workgroups, 1, 1);
findings.derivation: 3070 Ti Laptop: 5888 cores / 128 = 46 SMs, compute capability 8.6, 1536 threads per SM. 8192 threads = 256 warps, /46 = 5.6 warps per SM, 11.6%. 32768 threads = 22.3 warps per SM, 46%. Both fit in a single wave if register use is <= 64 per thread. Per step there are about 170 scatterer iterations of roughly 12-15 instructions plus an L1 load each, plus 16 thickness loads. With about 1.4 warps per scheduler at 8K there is little latency hiding. At 32K there are about 5.6 warps per scheduler, so issue throughput becomes the limit. Expected wall-time ratio for 32K vs 8K is about 1.5-2.5x, not 4x [estimated, requires measurement]. There is no tail waste: 8192 % 64 = 0, and the clear and drainage grids divide exactly by 16.

findings.recommendation: Keep @workgroup_size(64). Close or re-scope #37 to 'occupancy and ray-count scaling'. Pick num_rays by backend (e.g. 8K on GL/CPU adapters, 32K+ on discrete GPUs, using adapter.get_info().device_type). Re-measure on Dozen/native once gpuperf-04 is fixed. findings.title: Patch-mode spawn mapping uses a chord projection; the default patch centre lies on the gnomonic horizon of the default entry point, so ~0% of deposits reach the left half of the patch
findings.claim: Ray positions are gnomonic coordinates, pos_3d = normalize(entry + t1*x + t2*y), but the patch offset is the chord p - entry projected on (t1,t2). For the defaults (entry (0,0,1) from set_entry_point(90 deg, 0 deg) via pipeline.rs:1654-1655 and 1822, patch centre u=v=0.5, i.e. (1,0,0)), the offset is (-1,0), which maps to 45 degrees from entry (u=0.625), not to the 90-degree patch centre. A point 90 degrees away is at infinity in gnomonic coordinates, so patch points with phi < 0 can never be reached.
findings.derivation: t1 = normalize(cross((0,0,1),(0,1,0))) = (-1,0,0) and t2 = cross(entry,t1) = (0,-1,0). to_patch = (1,0,-1), so offset = (-1,0). normalize(entry - t1) = (0.707,0,0.707) gives phi = 45 deg, u = 0.625, local u = (0.625-0.342)/0.316 = 0.90. The replica prints the same spawn centre. The gnomonic inverse would be (p.t1, p.t2)/(p.entry) with p.entry = 0. Replica (patch, defaults): single-frame texel coverage 5.5%, left half (local u<0.5) 0.000, right half 0.110. Rays drift only 0.3 units (gpuperf-05), so they occupy roughly local u 0.82-1.0. The gnomonic parameterisation also has non-uniform arc length per unit of pos_2d (ds = dx*cos^2 along the radial direction), which biases the step_factor energy weighting away from entry.
findings.impact: With the default laser, the default patch view shows branched flow only in a narrow strip on its right edge. GPU texture area and fragment work on the rest of the patch show nothing.
findings.recommendation: Spawn with the gnomonic inverse, clamped to a horizon margin, or better, switch the propagation to the exponential map (pos_3d = cos|x| entry + sin|x| x_hat), which covers the whole sphere and moves geodesics at unit speed. Alternatively default the laser entry to the patch centre. This changes the loop body: test per gpuperf-08. Verify visually at defaults before changing anything, because this result comes from the replica, not from the running app.

verification.reasoning: The spawn math is identical to branched-03 and I re-derived it: t1 = (-1,0,0), t2 = (0,-1,0), offset (-1,0), u = 0.625, local u = 0.90. The geometric point that the patch's φ<0 half lies on the back hemisphere is right: z = sinθ·sinφ < 0, while gnomonic points always have z = 1/|q| > 0. That half is unreachable. As in branched-03, geomfoam-01 means the rendered patch currently shows no branched flow at all. The replica coverage fractions were not reproduced here.
verification.corrected_claim: The chord-projection spawn and the unreachable φ<0 half of the patch are real defects. The stated impact ('branched flow only in a narrow strip on its right edge') will appear only after geomfoam-01 is fixed. Today the patch view shows 0% branched flow, because the patch mesh is rendered 180° from where the shaders look. A visual check at defaults would therefore show nothing.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md 'GPU freeze, DO NOT RETRY' note is stale and its root cause was most likely llvmpipe workload, not a GPU hang
findings.claim: The current loop already contains a data-dependent break (wgsl:549-551), and patch spawning already places rays at the patch (wgsl:459-476). The kernel has no workgroupBarrier or storageBarrier, so there is no barrier-in-divergent-control-flow hazard; naga's uniformity analysis would reject that at shader creation rather than hang. At the commit that recorded the freeze (95191fc, 'Moving ray entry point to patch center caused GPU freezes'), the defaults were 32768 rays x 400 steps with an O(n) loop over 800 scatterers. Moving rays into the patch also made every step deposit. On a CPU rasterizer this produces multi-second dispatches and heavily contended atomics, which looks like a freeze.

**Attempted optimizations that caused GPU freezes (DO NOT RETRY):**
- Modifying the propagation loop body (early break, entry point change mid-loop)
findings.derivation: git show 95191fc shows total_scatterer_force as 'for (var i = 0u; i < n; i++)' over all scatterers, plus the same 'if (dist > 2.5 || intensity < 0.01) { break; }'. That break was dead even then: max travel 400*0.005 = 2.0, plus a start offset of 0.2 or less, stays below 2.5, and 0.999^400 = 0.67. Work per frame = 32768*400*800 = 1.05e10 scatterer evaluations. Before the change, rays started far from the patch and rarely deposited (deposits happen only in-patch). After it, every step deposits, giving 32768*400*4 = 52M atomicAdds into a few thousand texels. On llvmpipe these are real CPU atomics with cache-line contention across cores. Today the scatterer loop is hashed and rays already start in the patch without trouble. The exact change that froze is not recorded, so this root cause is a plausible reconstruction, not proven.

findings.recommendation: Reword CLAUDE.md:111-113 and MEMORY.md: 'loop-body changes froze the WSL llvmpipe session (Jan 2026, O(n) scatterers, 32Kx400); retest on a hardware adapter'. findings.title: #36 (workgroup shared-memory deposits) is not viable as written; atomics are a minor cost; the viable variant is stratified ray order plus subgroup aggregation
findings.claim: The deposit target is 512x256 u32 = 512 KiB, far above the 16 KiB default max_compute_workgroup_storage_size, so a per-workgroup tile can hold only a tiny window. Rays get hash-random start positions per lane (wgsl:439-440), so lanes of one workgroup deposit far apart. Per frame there are about 6.55M atomicAdds onto about 7.6K distinct texels (roughly 860 per texel). The return values are unused, so these compile to fire-and-forget reductions. Estimated cost is about 0.15 ms on GA104, small next to the trace compute.
findings.code_quote: atomicAdd(&caustic_texture[idx00], u32(base_deposit * w00));
findings.derivation: Atomics = 8192 rays * 200 steps * 0.998 in-patch * 4 = 6.54M (replica). Texels touched = 5.8% * 131072 = 7.6K. Throughput estimate: about 32 L2 slices * about 1 atomic per clock * 1.4 GHz = 45 G/s, so 6.5M atomics take about 0.15 ms [estimated, requires measurement]. Within a collimated beam of 8192 rays about 0.5 tangent units wide, adjacent rays are 6e-5 units, about 0.016 texel, apart if indexed in order. With rand1 = (idx+0.5)/N, a 32-lane warp would span about 0.5 texel and could pre-reduce with subgroupAdd (wgpu 24 Features::SUBGROUP, supported on Vulkan, DX12 and Metal) before 4 atomics. Stratification does not change the scatterer-loop warp efficiency (0.998 either way, divergence.py), but it is a lower-discrepancy beam sampling.

findings.title: #35 (temporal accumulation) is effectively implemented by the 0.85 fade; the proposed double buffer is the same recurrence
findings.claim: Fading in place and then atomicAdd-ing new deposits computes S_{n+1} = 0.85*S_n + D_n. That is an unnormalized exponential moving average with an effective window of 1/(1-0.85) = 6.7 frames, settling to 95% in about 18 frames (ln 0.05 / ln 0.85). #35's proposal B = alpha*A + (1-alpha)*new is the same recurrence scaled by the constant (1-alpha), at the cost of a second 512 KiB buffer and a blend pass.

findings.title: Airy reflectance gets an extra +pi phase: every interference fringe is inverted (cross-dimension optics finding)
findings.claim: The LUT, the legacy spectral shader paths and the CPU reference all add a pi (lambda/2) phase and then apply the Airy formula F sin^2(d/2)/(1+F sin^2(d/2)) [equivalently 2R(1-cos d)/(1+R^2-2R cos d)]. For a free-standing film (air|film|air) the Airy form already contains the half-wave flip through r23=-r12. Adding pi shifts the pattern by half a fringe period, so a 0 nm film is maximally bright and a quarter-wave film is black. This is the opposite of real thin-film behavior and of the Newton black film.
findings.derivation: Exact slab: r = (r12 + r23 e^{i d})/(1 + r12 r23 e^{i d}) with r23 = -r12 and d = 4 pi n h cos(theta_t)/lambda. Then |r|^2 = 2R(1-cos d)/(1+R^2-2R cos d) = F sin^2(d/2)/(1+F sin^2(d/2)) with R=r12^2 and F=4R/(1-R)^2. This vanishes at h=0. The two-beam convention 'OPD = 2nh cos + lambda/2, bright when OPD = m lambda' (docs/physics-reference.md:12-30) pairs with a cos^2 law, not with Airy's sin^2, so combining the two double-counts the flip. Numeric check (scratchpad sota/airy_phase_check.py, n=1.33, lambda=550, normal incidence) for h = 0 / 103.4 / 206.8 nm: exact = 0.000 / 0.077 / 0.000; code(+pi) = 0.077 / 0.000 / 0.077; code without pi = 0.000 / 0.077 / 0.000, matching exact to 5 decimals at all 9 thicknesses tested. Spectral impact (sota/spectral_check.py) against a dense 1 nm reference: mean chromaticity error |dxy| = 0.289 (max 0.442) for h in [30,600) nm with +pi, versus 0.056 without it.
findings.impact: The main path uses this LUT (bubble.wgsl:424-440), so the rendered interference colors at the default 500 nm, and for every other thickness, follow the wrong (complementary) fringe order. The 'thickness < 30 nm returns dark' override (bubble.wgsl:515-517) masks the most obvious symptom, a bright zero-thickness film.

Add a unit test asserting R(h=0)=0 and R(h=lambda/(4n))=max. Document the convention in docs/physics-reference.md and the CLAUDE.md 'Core Physics' line. This lies outside the SOTA dimension; dedupe against the optics auditor.

findings.title: Interference LUT: 7-wavelength sampling aliases above ~680 nm and the CIE fit mixes the Wyman 2013 left/right sigmas
findings.claim: The LUT is precomputed once on the CPU, yet it integrates only 7 wavelengths (50 nm spacing) across a 0-2000 nm thickness axis, and it uses the Wyman-Sloan-Shirley 2013 multi-lobe CIE means with symmetric Gaussians (mostly the left-side sigma, but the right-side sigma for the y-bar 530.9 lobe). Both errors are free to fix because the cost is paid only at LUT build time. Belcour & Barla 2017-style analytic spectral pre-integration is unnecessary here, since the LUT already is the pre-integration.
findings.derivation: Aliasing: the interference term is periodic in wavenumber k=1/lambda with period 1/(2nh). Sampling is alias-free while 2*pi*2nh*dk < pi, i.e. h < 1/(4 n dk). For the 400/450 nm pair dk=2.78e-4 nm^-1, so h < 677 nm; for the 650/700 nm pair h < 1711 nm. The LUT spans 0-2000 nm (bubble.wgsl:64), so the upper two-thirds of its domain aliases in blue. CIE: Wyman 2013 Table 1 gives inverse sigmas, e.g. z-bar lobe at 437 nm uses beta=0.0845 (sigma_left=11.8) and gamma=0.0278 (sigma_right=36.0); the code uses 11.8 on both sides, so z-bar(450) = 1.305 vs 1.781 and y-bar(500) = 0.455 vs 0.328 (sota/spectral_check.py). An equal-energy spectrum through the code's 7-sample CIE lands at xy = (0.365, 0.383) instead of about (0.333, 0.333), a yellow-green cast. The dense 1 nm Wyman fit gives (0.3330, 0.3337). Mean |dxy| against the dense reference (no-pi physics): code sigmas 0.056 / 0.079 / 0.112 for h in [30,600) / [600,1200) / [1200,2000) nm; correct sigmas with 7 samples 0.010 / 0.052 / 0.114, so the residual above 600 nm is aliasing. Per-row signs differ, so no single summary number is given.
findings.impact: A color cast on all films, plus wrong hues for thick films (more than ~680 nm, reached as drainage thickens the bottom). Zero runtime cost to fix.
findings.recommendation: In generate_interference_lut, integrate 380-780 nm at 1-5 nm (81-401 samples) with tabulated CIE 1931 2-degree CMFs or the full asymmetric Wyman fit (Listing 1). Normalize so the equal-energy white maps to the D65/E white. Consider an Rgba16Float LUT (it is Rgba8Unorm at pipeline.rs:411, linear data in 8 bits) and more thickness samples (256 over 2000 nm = 7.8 nm per texel). Optionally prefilter the LUT along h (mip chain) to anti-alias sub-pixel thickness variation, which is the practical real-time core of Belcour & Barla 2017 and Kneiphof et al. 2019.

findings.title: GPU drainage dt never reaches the shader; the field stays essentially uniform, and wiring dt naively breaks the explicit stability limit near the poles
findings.claim: step() computes step_dt from frame dt, time_scale and steps_per_frame, but only adds it to current_time. The uniform keeps its initial dt = 0.001 s because set_dt()/update_params() have zero callers. Physics therefore advances 10 x 1 ms per frame regardless of the time_scale/steps sliders, while the displayed clock runs about 167x faster. Combined with uniform initial thickness/concentration and the tiny coded drainage rate, the thickness buffer that drives the branched-flow GRIN force stays practically uniform. Once dt is wired as intended, FTCS on the 256x128 lat-long grid becomes unstable in the first rows next to the poles.
findings.derivation: rg finds `set_dt(` and `gpu_drainage...update_params` only at their definitions (gpu_drainage.rs:385,391). pipeline.rs:1408 calls step(&mut encoder, last_dt) only. Displayed vs simulated time per frame at defaults (time_scale 100, 10 steps, 60 fps): (1/60)*100 = 1.667 s vs 10*0.001 = 0.01 s, a factor of about 167. Coded rate at h=500 nm: rho g h^3/(3 eta) = 1000*9.81*(5e-7)^3/3e-3 = 4.1e-13 (units m^2/s, see sota-05), i.e. about 4e-6 nm per frame and about 0.15 nm after 10 min at 60 fps. Initial thickness and concentration are uniform (gpu_drainage.rs:127,131), so the Marangoni and diffusion terms start at zero. Stability (sota/drainage_stability.py): dx_theta = R dtheta = 6.18e-4 m; dx_phi at row 1 = R sin(dtheta) dphi = 1.52e-5 m, 40x smaller than at the equator. The FTCS limit dt <= 1/(2D(1/dx_theta^2 + 1/dx_phi^2)) with D=1e-9 is 95 s at the equator and 0.115 s at row 1, an 824x polar penalty. Intended step_dt = 0.167 s gives dt/limit = 1.45 (unstable); time_scale 500 with 1 step gives 72x. If the physically correct 4th-order capillary term were added (mobility gamma h^3/(3 eta), gamma=0.03), the row-1 explicit limit is 1.3 ms against 3.5e3 s at the equator.
findings.impact: The UI's time_scale and steps sliders are inert for the physics. The GPU drainage produces no visible structure, so the GRIN part of branched flow (weight 1 - particle_weight = 0.9) sees about zero gradient and branching comes only from scatterers (relevant to #39). Visual consequence estimated, not run. #31 ('actual frame dt for drainage dispatch') is only half done.
findings.recommendation: Upload step_dt each frame (queue.write_buffer of params.dt before the passes). Before raising dt, remove the polar CFL with a cheap scheme first: treat the phi-direction term implicitly per latitude ring (periodic tridiagonal, 256 unknowns, one workgroup per row via parallel cyclic reduction, Zhang-Cohen-Owens 2010) and keep theta explicit, which leaves the equator-scale ~95 s limit. Alternatively apply polar Fourier filtering. A cube-sphere (Putman & Lin 2007) or icosahedral grid removes the pole problem but means rewriting the sampling in bubble.wgsl and branched_flow_compute.wgsl. Not worth it at 256x128. Multigrid on lat-long needs line relaxation because of the anisotropy; prefer ADI or line-implicit. Also seed non-uniform initial thickness (or a Huang 2020 equilibrium profile) so the GRIN force has structure.

verification.reasoning: Duplicate of drainage-02 and cpuperf-05 for the dt plumbing. Grep confirms set_dt and update_params are defined only (gpu_drainage.rs:385, :391), and pipeline.rs:1408 calls only step(..., last_dt). I recomputed the stability numbers: dxθ = 6.184e-4 m and dxφ(row 1) = 1.518e-5 m, giving FTCS limits of 0.115 s at row 1 and 94.9 s at the equator (824×). 0.167/0.115 = 1.45 and 8.33/0.115 = 72, both check. particle_weight defaults to 0.1 (branched_flow.rs:137), so the GRIN weight is 0.9, which checks. Corrections: the '0.15 nm after 10 min' estimate ignores f32. The actual change is exactly zero, because each per-step increment is below half an ulp (drainage-02), so the field is exactly uniform rather than 'practically' uniform. The side remark on the capillary limit uses the isotropic dx^4/(32M). For row 1, where dxφ dominates, the limit is dxφ^4/(8M) ≈ 5 ms rather than 1.3 ms. Neither correction affects the conclusion. Zhang-Cohen-Owens and Putman-Lin citations are unverified here.

findings.title: Drainage model vs SOTA: the coded gravity term is a flux used as a rate; Huang 2020's reduced model fits the existing lat-long grid
findings.claim: The drainage term -rho g h^3 sin(theta)/(3 eta) has units m^2/s. It is the lubrication flux q_theta, not dh/dt. Thinning is -div_s q, which is mass-conserving: it thins the top and thickens the bottom. The code instead thins everywhere, fastest at the equator, and is about 2/R = 80x too small in magnitude scale. Current SOTA (Huang 2020, Ishida 2020, Deng 2022, Tang 2024) evolves thickness by conservative transport driven by a surface velocity field.
findings.code_quote:
drainage.wgsl:132: let drainage_coeff = params.density * params.gravity / (3.0 * params.viscosity);
drainage.wgsl:136: let drainage_term = -drainage_coeff * h_cubed * sin_theta;
findings.derivation: Dimensions: [rho g/(3 eta)] = (kg m^-3 m s^-2)/(Pa s) = m^-1 s^-1; multiplied by h^3 (m^3) this gives m^2/s, i.e. volume flux per unit length. Conservation on a sphere: dh/dt = -(1/(R sin theta)) d/dtheta(sin theta q_theta) with q_theta = (rho g h^3/(3 eta)) sin theta (gravity component along e_theta for north pole up). For uniform h: dh/dt = -(rho g h^3/(3 eta R)) (1/sin theta) d/dtheta(sin^2 theta) = -(2 rho g h^3/(3 eta R)) cos theta. This is negative (thinning) for theta < pi/2 and positive below the equator; the scale ratio to the coded term is 2/R = 80 for R = 0.025 m (sota/drainage_stability.py). Literature: Huang et al. 2020 (references/Huang_2020_Chemomechanical_soap_film.pdf, sec. 4) uses a staggered lat-long grid, BiMocq2 advection extended to spherical coordinates with a flow-aligned frame for poles, and an implicit, CG-solved update for Gamma. Reported cost: 1024x2048 grid, dt 0.002 s, 16-17 CG iterations, 1.1 s per step on a GTX 1080 with CUDA+AmgX. Ishida et al. 2020 (TOG 39(4):31) evolves thickness on non-manifold triangle meshes. Deng et al. 2022 MELP (TOG 41(4):154) uses particles. Tang et al. 2024 (vortex particle-on-mesh, SIGGRAPH 2024) couples circulation, surfactant and thickness. Heiss-Synak 2025 (ISTA thesis) is a surface-only bubble-cluster plus thickness solver.
findings.impact: The thickness patterns are not physical drainage (no bottom accumulation), even after sota-04 is fixed.
findings.recommendation: Short term: rewrite the gravity term in finite-volume flux form on the staggered theta faces (sin-weighted). This conserves mass and gives top-thin/bottom-thick, about 30 WGSL lines. Medium term: port Huang 2020's reduced model (u, Gamma, eta on the same 256x128 grid; semi-Lagrangian/BiMocq2 advection plus matrix-free CG for the Gamma/u implicit step in WGSL). The grid has 64x fewer cells than Huang's 1024x2048, so interactive rates on a dGPU are plausible [estimated, requires measurement]. Cost: about 500-1000 WGSL/Rust lines. Ishida, MELP and Tang need mesh or particle infrastructure and do not fit this codebase. Overlaps the physics auditor; dedupe.

verification.reasoning: Duplicate of drainage-03 for the physics. drainage.wgsl:132,136 verified. Units are m^2/s. The conservative form with a 3η flux gives -(2ρg h^3/(3ηR))·cosθ, and the ratio to the coded term is 2/R = 80, which I re-derived. Literature I checked in the repo PDF: Huang 2020 §4.4 (p.7) states CUDA + AmgX on a GTX 1080, 1024×2048 grid, 0.002 s step, 16-17 CG iterations and 1.1 s per step, all verbatim. BiMocq^2 (§4.2.1) and the velocity-aligned pole frame (§4.2, Fig. 8-9) are confirmed, as is the implicit CG solve for Γ (eq. 26). The claims about Ishida 2020, Deng 2022 MELP, Tang 2024 and Heiss-Synak 2025 are not in the repo and were not verified. The 'about 30 WGSL lines' and '500-1000 lines' cost estimates are unmeasured.

findings.title: Branched flow: keep the ray model, but bend rays with grad n_eff(d) (slab-waveguide index), not grad d; BPM is the wave-optics upgrade path
findings.claim: Patsyk 2020 attributes branching to variations of the waveguide effective index n_eff(d), which become substantial only near 1-2 wavelengths of thickness. The shader instead bends rays by the raw thickness gradient times a constant bend_strength, and dn_eff/dd varies about 200x between 100 nm and 2 um. Patsyk 2022 shows the main branches are ray-optics caustics that survive with incoherent light, while interference sidelobes are coherent. The ray approach is therefore the right first-order model; a split-step Fourier BPM would only add sidelobes. Secondary: the gradient weights the phi component 2x relative to theta, because u = phi/(2 pi) but v = theta/pi.
findings.derivation: Ray equation in a 2D GRIN medium: d/ds(n dr/ds) = grad n, so the curvature is |grad_perp n|/n = (dn_eff/dd)|grad_perp d|/n_eff. TE0 of a symmetric slab (n=1.33 in air, lambda=532 nm) solves kappa tan(kappa d/2) = gamma (sota/slab_neff.py). Results: n_eff = 1.074 / 1.274 / 1.311 / 1.325 at d = 100 / 500 / 1000 / 2000 nm, with dn_eff/dd = 1.08 / 0.159 / 0.0315 / 0.0051 per um. The correct bending strength therefore changes 5x between 500 nm and 1 um at the same thickness gradient. Anisotropy: normal_to_uv (lines 108-113) gives u = (phi+pi)/(2 pi) and v = theta/pi, so dh/du = 2 pi dh/dphi and dh/dv = pi dh/dtheta. grad_x = 2 pi (1/sin theta) dh/dphi and grad_y = pi dh/dtheta, whereas the surface gradient on the unit sphere is ((1/sin theta) dh/dphi, dh/dtheta). The phi force is overweighted 2x. Line 242 clamps u instead of wrapping, so the phi=±pi seam has a one-sided difference. Literature: Patsyk et al. 2022 PRX 12, 021007 simulate with the paraxial wave equation and state that the main channels are caustics (ray optics) and the sidelobes come from interference. Ding, Wang, Yang 2023 (Photonics Research 11, 1992) treat branched flow on constant-Gaussian-curvature surfaces (positive curvature moves the first branching point earlier). Garnier, Picozzi, Torres 2025 give a stochastic paraxial theory.
findings.impact: Bending is wrongly weighted with thickness and direction, so branch statistics such as first-caustic distance do not follow physical scaling. Low visual risk at current defaults because the drainage field is nearly uniform (sota-04).
findings.recommendation: Precompute a 1D LUT of n_eff(d) (TE0, optionally per RGB wavelength) and use force = n_eff'(d) grad d / n_eff, either at sample time or by storing n_eff in the buffer. Divide the u-difference by 2 pi and the v-difference by pi (or scale grad_x by 1/2 relative to grad_y). Wrap u modulo 1 in sample_thickness_at_uv. The setup-only and force-function changes stay outside the propagation loop body, as CLAUDE.md requires. Wave-optics path (optional, high cost): a paraxial split-step Fourier BPM along the beam in a local chart, needing a WGSL radix-2 Stockham FFT (wgpu has no FFT primitive). It is only worthwhile to show coherent sidelobes. Relates to #26 and #39.

verification.reasoning: Code facts verified. The thickness gradient is raw and scaled by a constant bend_strength (:284-286, :530). The 2:1 φ/θ weighting comes from u = φ/2π and v = θ/π (:108-113), duplicating branched-08. :242 clamps uv.x instead of wrapping, so the φ = ±π seam gets a one-sided difference. I spot-checked the TE0 slab values with my own solve at 532 nm: n_eff = 1.0741 at 100 nm and 1.2746 at 500 nm, matching the finder's 1.074 and 1.274. The 1000 and 2000 nm values and the dn_eff/dd figures were not reproduced. The phrase 'variations become substantial only near 1-2 wavelengths' is muddled, since the finder's own numbers show dn_eff/dd largest for thin films. Patsyk 2022, Ding 2023 and Garnier 2025 are not in the repo and were not verified. Low because the GRIN path is currently dead (branched-01, drainage-02), as the finding itself notes.

findings.title: Do not move compute to CUDA: no graphics interop on WSL, small workload, and the Rust CUDA stacks are early-stage. CubeCL on a shared wgpu device is the only zero-copy Rust-kernel option
findings.claim: For a real-time renderer that already runs WGSL compute on the same wgpu device, CUDA would add a host round-trip per frame on WSL, a second toolchain, and NVIDIA lock-in, for a workload that is small on any discrete GPU. Of the Rust GPU-compute crates, only CubeCL can share the renderer's wgpu device (needs wgpu 30).

findings.title: #36/#37 on hardware: subgroup aggregation is available; per-workgroup tiles need ray/deposit binning first
findings.claim: #36's shared-memory deposits cannot hold the whole 512x256 u32 texture (512 KiB), against a wgpu default limit of 16 KiB and dzn's 32 KiB. They need tile binning of rays or deposits. A cheaper first step is warp-aggregated atomics through subgroup ops: neighbouring ray indices in a collimated beam often hit the same texels. On the measured dzn NVIDIA adapter these ops are available with subgroupSize 32, but GLES has none, so the path must be feature-gated. #37 tuning is meaningless until #38 is resolved.

branched_flow_compute.wgsl:405: @compute @workgroup_size(64)
branched_flow_compute.wgsl:369: let fx = clamp(uv.x, 0.0, 1.0) * f32(params.tex_width - 1u);
findings.derivation: wgpu-types-24.0.0/src/lib.rs:1284 default max_compute_workgroup_storage_size = 16384. vulkaninfo for dzn NVIDIA: maxComputeSharedMemorySize = 32768, subgroupSize = 32, ops BASIC/VOTE/ARITHMETIC/BALLOT/SHUFFLE/SHUFFLE_RELATIVE/QUAD. A 64x64 u32 tile = 16 KiB fits; the full texture is 32x too large. The workgroup size of 64 is 2 subgroups of 32 on NVIDIA and 1 wave64 on AMD.
